chunks: "It's the silkscreen, also called the legend or nomenclature. It's a layer of ink, usually white epoxy ink, printed on top of the soldermask.

It carries the human-readable information: reference designators like R1 and U3, outlines of the components, polarity marks and pin-1 dots, test point names, connector labels, board name and revision, logos, and sometimes regulatory markings.
It's called silkscreen because it used to be applied through a fine mesh screen; today many fabs use direct inkjet printing, which has finer resolution. A few design rules matter.
Keep the ink off the pads and vias, because ink on a pad prevents soldering, and the fab will clip it anyway, cutting your text.
Use a reasonable text height and line width, about a millimetre and 0. 15 millimetre as a typical minimum, depending on the fab.
Make the text readable in one or two orientations and put it where it won't be hidden under the component.
And pick the colour for contrast: white on green or black, black on white or yellow mask.
It's what makes a board assemblable and debuggable, so I always include polarity and pin-1 marks and label the test points."
